provenance.triage_rule_map: FP-01..FP-13 are the 13 negative constraints from mantis-review/SKILL.md, in that skill's own order: FP-01 ignore hypothetical misuse; FP-02 ignore missing hygiene / defense-in-depth; FP-03 require strict reproducibility; FP-04 avoid pedantic linting; FP-05 no security-flaw stretching on mitigations; FP-06 evaluate questionable file paths; FP-07 ignore resource-exhaustion DoS; FP-08 intrinsic security flaws count even if uncalled; FP-09 verify mitigations pragmatically; FP-10 refine code_paths strictly; FP-11 ignore SIMD/vector padding; FP-12 ensure source-code coherence (anti-hallucination); FP-13 verify attacker control of the source. answer semantics: HOLDS = the disqualifier applies to this finding; DOES_NOT_HOLD = checked and it does not; UNKNOWN = could not resolve it, and the severity reflects that; NOT_APPLICABLE = the rule does not bear on this class of bug. Only rules that bear on a given finding are listed. FP-11 bears on nothing in this tree (no SIMD or vector code in any of the six components) and is therefore omitted throughout.

ruled_out.assertion: ORDER BY is interpolated into raw SQL in the permit listing
ruled_out.killed_by: The sort value is bounced through PermitSort(rawValue:) at line 57 and the request is rejected if it does not match; every other interpolation in the query uses \(bind:). The mitigation works, so this is not injection.

ruled_out.assertion: CORS is set to .all with allowCredentials true
ruled_out.killed_by: Only outside production (PORTAL_ENV != production), and the API authenticates with bearer tokens rather than ambient cookies, so a wildcard origin is not a credential-theft path on its own. Noted as a reach amplifier for the /internal finding, not filed separately.

ruled_out.assertion: DB_PASSWORD defaults to an empty string and loopback TLS is disabled
ruled_out.killed_by: A default for an unset environment variable is not a stored credential, and the loopback TLS exemption is bounded to 127.0.0.1/localhost by the branch at line 17.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the catalog Search path
ruled_out.killed_by: Search takes ORDER BY from the sortableColumns allowlist via ParseOrderBy and clamps LIMIT/OFFSET to integers at server.go:172-178 and :222-233. Only the export path abandons that, which is filed separately.

ruled_out.assertion: The grpc-gateway listens in plaintext on :8080
ruled_out.killed_by: No in-tree evidence of what fronts the listener; asserting exposure would be inventing a deployment. Left unfiled rather than guessed.

ruled_out.assertion: Consul intentions are ordered so the wildcard deny never applies
ruled_out.killed_by: The ordering is correct: explicit sources are listed ahead of the trailing wildcard deny, which is how Consul evaluates them. The mitigation works as written.

ruled_out.assertion: The Traefik admin entrypoint exposes an unauthenticated dashboard
ruled_out.killed_by: Grep found no --api or --api.insecure flag anywhere in the job; the dashboard is not enabled, so the claim had no line to stand on.

ruled_out.assertion: Nomad client ACLs are disabled and gossip is plaintext
ruled_out.killed_by: acl { enabled = true } and mutual TLS are both genuinely configured in the baseline. These are working mitigations.

ruled_out.assertion: Vector ships secret-bearing log fields to the shared S3 bucket
ruled_out.killed_by: The redact transform feeds the only S3 sink, so the stated control is on the path the data actually takes.

ruled_out.assertion: SFTP host key verification is disabled
ruled_out.killed_by: load_host_keys is called and the policy is RejectPolicy, not AutoAddPolicy. This is the correct configuration.

ruled_out.assertion: Unsafe deserialization or command execution in the pipeline
ruled_out.killed_by: Grep for pickle, yaml.load, eval, exec, shell=True, zipfile and tarfile returns nothing across the component. There is no such construct to cite.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal from remote SFTP filenames when writing downloads
ruled_out.killed_by: Remote names pass through os.path.basename and the downloads land in a BytesIO buffer rather than on disk, so there is no filesystem join to traverse.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in the ledger posting statements
ruled_out.killed_by: Every statement in the module is parameterised with %s placeholders through psycopg. The COPY buffer is a separate defect and is filed on its own terms, not as SQL injection.

ruled_out.assertion: The quarantine markdown artifact writes raw account numbers past the log redaction filter
ruled_out.killed_by: In the production (lenient) configuration nothing is ever quarantined, so quarantine_rows is always empty and the block never executes. Filing it would mean claiming a path that the shipped configuration cannot reach.

ruled_out.assertion: Redaction can be bypassed so PII reaches the model
ruled_out.killed_by: crawlSource maps redactChunk over every chunk at crawler.ts:64, and indexChunks has no other caller, so the module's claim that everything indexed has been through it holds for this tree.

ruled_out.assertion: The vector store leaks across workspaces
ruled_out.killed_by: searchChunks, listDocuments and deleteDocument all filter on workspaceId (lines 64, 82 and 109). The tenant dimension is present everywhere in this file.

ruled_out.assertion: SSRF via the crawler's URL parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: The primary flaw class is blocked: the scheme must be https and the hostname must be in ALLOWED_HOSTS. The residual gap is that maxRedirections: 2 does not re-apply the allowlist to redirect targets, but reaching it requires already controlling an approved documentation host, at which point corpus injection is the easier path. Left unfiled rather than inflated.

ruled_out.assertion: XSS in the sitewatch report notes renderer
ruled_out.killed_by: renderNotes calls escapeHtml before applying the bold and italic substitutions, so the capture groups only ever contain already-escaped text and there is no attribute context. The mitigation is correctly ordered.

ruled_out.assertion: webSecurity is disabled and a QA marker file can turn it off in a shipped build
ruled_out.killed_by: isDevMode returns true for a dev.flag file in the user-data directory (config.js:42), but nothing reachable from the renderer can create that file - settings:set writes into the electron-store document and the plugin writes are confined to plugins/<name>-<version>.js. It needs an attacker who already has local filesystem write, so it is a hardening note rather than a finding.

findings.title: AdminController is registered under /internal on the public listener with no authentication
findings.evidence: routes.swift:45-46 is `let internalRoutes = app.grouped("internal")` followed by `try internalRoutes.register(collection: AdminController())`. The public group three lines above chains both middlewares (`.grouped(RateLimitMiddleware(...)).grouped(BearerAuthMiddleware())`, routes.swift:35-38); the internal group chains neither. configure.swift builds one Application and serves one listener (Entrypoint.main, configure.swift:83-92) -- there is no second port, no bind address restriction and no IP filter, so the comment's claim that the caseworker client 'talks to the service over the council LAN rather than through the public edge' is not enforced anywhere in the code. AdminController.boot exposes four routes (AdminController.swift:23-26), including `GET /internal/permits/export?tenant=<uuid>` which filters solely on the caller-supplied tenant query parameter (AdminController.swift:49-52).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated request to /internal/permits/export?tenant=<uuid> dumps every permit row for any council; /internal/permits/:id/approve mutates a permit's status, reviewer and internal review notes with no token and no tenant check; /internal/sessions/active and /internal/attachments/import are equally open. This is full cross-tenant read and write on the primary record store from the internet.
findings.recommendation: Register AdminController behind BearerAuthMiddleware plus an explicit role check, or bind it to a separate internal listener. Derive the export tenant from the authenticated session rather than the query string.

triage.reason: Not missing-hygiene: this is the absence of the primary authentication control on a data-plane route group, not a hardening nicety.
One unauthenticated HTTP request reproduces it; no timing, no race, no unusual environment.
Not a test or mock path -- routes() is the production route tree called from configure.swift:74.
There is no mitigation to credit: I looked for a network-level one and found none in the tree.
Re-read: routes.swift:45 and :46 are as quoted; AdminController.swift:21-27 defines the four routes.
Not a data-flow taint finding; the missing control is structural.

scope.established_by: app.grouped("internal") creates a route group off the same Application with no middleware chained, and AdminController is registered into it.
scope.narrowed_by: Nothing in this tree. The only stated control is a deployment assumption written in a comment (routes.swift:43-44).

searched.found: nothing - one Application, one app.execute(), no hostname or port restriction beyond defaults

findings.title: Permit listing cache key omits the tenant, so one council's permit list is served to another
findings.class: cross-tenant data exposure via cache key collision (CWE-524)
findings.evidence: The key is built as `"permits:list:\(status ?? "any"):\(page):\(perPage)"` (PermitController.swift:44) -- status, page and per-page only. The query the cache memoises is explicitly tenant-scoped (`WHERE tenant_id = \(bind: user.tenantID)`, PermitController.swift:61) and the projection is stored back under the same tenant-free key (PermitController.swift:69). ResponseCache is a single process-wide actor (`static let shared`, ResponseCache.swift:9) with a 45-second TTL (ResponseCache.swift:17), so the first council to request page 1 populates the entry and every other council asking for the same page within 45 seconds gets that payload returned at PermitController.swift:45-46 before any query runs.
findings.impact: Any authenticated staff user reads another council's permit list -- applicant details, addresses and statuses -- with no crafted input at all, just the default dashboard request. The dashboards poll every few seconds, so the collision is continuous rather than incidental.
findings.recommendation: Include user.tenantID in the cache key, and make ResponseCache.invalidate operate on the tenant-qualified prefix.

triage.reason: Not caller misuse: the key is constructed inside list() and the caller supplies only ordinary pagination parameters.
Deterministic within the 45s TTL; two tenants polling the same dashboard page reproduce it without effort.
Not pedantic linting -- no safe library is doing the scoping; the tenant dimension is simply absent from the key string.
The tenant filter on the SQL is a real mitigation and I credit it; the point is that a cache hit returns before that SQL executes.
Re-read: PermitController.swift:44 is the cacheKey assignment, :45 the hit check, :69 the store; ResponseCache.swift:9 is `static let shared`.
Ingress: the status/page/perPage query parameters at PermitController.swift:41-43 are attacker-chosen and are the whole key, so an attacker picks which entry to collide with.

scope.established_by: The tenant-free key string plus ResponseCache.shared being a single process-global dictionary rather than a per-tenant store.
scope.narrowed_by: 45-second TTL and a 512-entry cap (ResponseCache.swift:17-18) bound how long and how many stale cross-tenant payloads persist.

searched.for: any tenant partitioning inside the cache itself
searched.found: nothing - entries is a flat [String: Entry] and value(for:) does a bare dictionary lookup

searched.for: other ResponseCache call sites that might key correctly and prove intent
searched.found: only list() reads and writes it; detail() at line 71 onward queries directly with the tenant filter

searched.for: invalidation that might narrow the window
searched.found: invalidate(prefix: "permits:list:") at AdminController.swift:44 clears every tenant's entries on any approval - it does not scope by tenant either

findings.title: PUT /attachments/:id/content never checks the attachment belongs to the caller's tenant
findings.evidence: replaceContent opens with `_ = try req.auth.require(StaffUser.self)` (AttachmentController.swift:109) -- it discards the authenticated user rather than binding it -- then loads the attachment and writes the new bytes (AttachmentController.swift:120-121). The private loader it uses does a bare primary-key lookup with no tenant predicate (`Attachment.find(id, on: req.db)`, AttachmentController.swift:71). Its three siblings in the same file all re-fetch the parent permit and compare `permit.tenantID == user.tenantID`: metadata at :81-82, download at :92-93 and remove at :133-134. replaceContent is the only handler in the collection missing that comparison.
findings.impact: An authenticated staff user of one council overwrites the stored content and content-type of any attachment belonging to another council, given its identifier -- destroying or substituting evidence attached to a permit case.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same parent-permit tenant check the sibling handlers use, and bind the authenticated user instead of discarding it.

triage.reason: Not caller misuse: the check is missing inside the handler, and the file itself shows the intended invariant three times over.
A single PUT with a known attachment id reproduces it.
Production controller registered on the authenticated api/v1 group at routes.swift:41.
code path narrowed to the handler that omits the check, not its correct siblings.
Re-read: AttachmentController.swift:109 is the discarding auth.require; :71 is the untenanted Attachment.find; :81, :92 and :133 carry the tenant comparison.
Ingress: the :attachmentID path parameter read at AttachmentController.swift:67, plus the request body decoded at :111.

scope.established_by: load() resolves an attachment by id alone and replaceContent does not re-scope it to the caller's tenant.
scope.narrowed_by: Attachment identifiers are UUIDs, so the caller needs the id out of band; the content-type allowlist and 8MB cap at :114-119 still apply to what is written.

searched.for: a tenant predicate inside load() that would make the per-handler checks redundant
searched.found: nothing - load() is Attachment.find(id) with no filter, which is why every other handler re-checks

searched.found: nothing found that would apply automatically

searched.for: a role gate that might keep ordinary staff off this route

findings.title: Credential endpoint /auth/token is registered outside the rate-limited group
findings.evidence: `app.post("auth", "token")` is registered directly on the Application at routes.swift:22, before and outside the group built at routes.swift:35-38 that chains `RateLimitMiddleware(limit: 120, window: 60)`. Every other client-facing route inherits that limiter through the api/v1 group. The handler runs a bcrypt comparison per attempt (BearerAuthMiddleware.swift:85) and returns a distinguishable 401 on failure (routes.swift:29), with no counter, lockout or backoff anywhere on the path.
findings.impact: Unlimited online password guessing and credential stuffing against staff accounts, at whatever rate bcrypt and the connection pool allow, with no signal that would trip the throttle the rest of the API has.
findings.recommendation: Chain RateLimitMiddleware (with a tighter limit) onto the token route and key it on the submitted username as well as the peer address.

triage.reason: Not defense-in-depth: the limiter exists in this component and is applied to every route except the one that checks passwords, which inverts the usual priority.
Reproducible by repeating a POST; nothing fragile about it.
Not a resource-exhaustion claim -- the harm is credential compromise, not service degradation.
Re-read: routes.swift:22 registers on `app`; the RateLimitMiddleware chain is at routes.swift:37 on a separate group.
Ingress: the TokenRequest body decoded at routes.swift:23.

scope.established_by: The route is attached to the bare Application while the limiter is attached to the api/v1 group.
scope.narrowed_by: Bcrypt verification cost bounds the achievable guess rate, and the account lookup still requires a valid username.

searched.for: a globally registered rate limiter in app.middleware.use
searched.found: only CORSMiddleware, ErrorMiddleware and FileMiddleware are registered globally

searched.for: a failed-attempt counter, lockout or delay in StaffDirectory.verify
searched.found: nothing - it is a single query plus Bcrypt.verify with no attempt tracking

findings.title: Rate-limit bucket is derived from the unverified Authorization header
findings.evidence: identity() returns `"tok:" + String(bearer.token.prefix(16))` whenever an Authorization header is present (RateLimitMiddleware.swift:37-38), and the middleware runs before BearerAuthMiddleware in the chain (routes.swift:37 then :38), so the token has not been validated at that point. A caller can therefore choose its own bucket by varying the header.
findings.impact: Bounded. An unauthenticated caller can rotate the header to get a fresh 120-request window per value, but the requests it unlocks are rejected by the auth middleware immediately afterwards, so the bypass buys throughput against endpoints that return 401. Rated low for that reason rather than as a hedge.
findings.recommendation: Key the bucket on the resolved session after authentication, and fall back to the peer address for unauthenticated requests.

triage.reason: The middleware itself chooses the key; no hypothetical caller is involved.
Arguably a hardening gap rather than a flaw, since the requests it unlocks still fail authentication -- this uncertainty is exactly why the severity is low.
Trivially reproducible by sending a different bearer value per request.
Re-read: RateLimitMiddleware.swift:37 is the bearerAuthorization check and :38 the prefix-16 key.

scope.established_by: The limiter is chained ahead of the authenticator and keys on the raw header.
scope.narrowed_by: Requests carrying a bogus token are still rejected by BearerAuthMiddleware, so the bypass does not reach any protected handler.

searched.for: the middleware ordering, to see whether authentication could run first
searched.found: RateLimitMiddleware is chained at :37 and BearerAuthMiddleware at :38, so the limiter is strictly earlier

searched.for: whether the peer-address fallback is reachable for a caller that wants a shared bucket
searched.found: only when no Authorization header is present at all

findings.title: BlobStore.putRestored joins a caller-supplied key onto the blob root with no shape check
findings.evidence: put() and get() both route the key through resolve(), which enforces a non-empty <=80 character `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$` key with no `..` (AttachmentController.swift:17-24). putRestored skips resolve entirely and calls `root.appendingPathComponent(key)` directly (AttachmentController.swift:45) before writing. The type comment states the omission is deliberate because 'the tarball index has already been checked'.
findings.impact: Whatever calls this can write outside the blob root. No caller exists anywhere in the tree, so nothing in this component is exploitable today; the exposure is the trap left for the restore tool that is meant to use it.
findings.recommendation: Route putRestored through resolve() as well, or validate the tarball index against the same shape rule at the point it is parsed.

triage.reason: This is precisely the hypothetical-caller case the rule describes: the flaw requires a future caller to pass a traversing key. I am reporting it anyway under FP-08 and marking the severity low to reflect that.
The unguarded path join is a direct injection path in this function's own logic, which the intrinsic-flaw carve-out keeps in scope even with no live caller.
Re-read: AttachmentController.swift:45 is `let url = root.appendingPathComponent(key)` with no preceding resolve().
No ingress point can be cited because no caller exists in this tree; that gap is the reason the status is probable rather than confirmed.

scope.established_by: putRestored bypasses the resolve() guard its two siblings use.
scope.narrowed_by: No caller in the repository, so there is no reachable path today.

searched.found: nothing - grep for putRestored matches only its definition

searched.for: whether the restore tool referenced in the comment lives in this tree
searched.found: nothing - the tool is described but not present

findings.title: ExportItems is a streaming RPC and no stream interceptor exists, so it runs unauthenticated with a client-named tenant
findings.evidence: main.go builds the server with `grpc.UnaryInterceptor(auth.Unary)` and nothing else (main.go:52); a repo-wide grep for StreamInterceptor, ChainStream or any grpc.ServerStream wrapper returns no matches. ExportItems is declared server-streaming in the contract (`rpc ExportItems(ExportRequest) returns (stream Item);`, proto/catalog.proto:81), so it is dispatched without ever entering AuthInterceptor.resolve. The handler then discards the lookup result -- `caller, _ := CallerFrom(ctx)` (server.go:204), where every unary handler checks the ok -- and when the resulting tenant is empty falls back to `metadataValue(ctx, "x-catalog-tenant")` (server.go:210), a value the client sets.
findings.impact: Any party that can open a TLS connection to the gRPC port streams the entire item table of any tenant it names, with no token at all. It is also the unauthenticated entry point for the SQL injection reported separately in store.ExportQuery.
findings.recommendation: Register a stream interceptor that runs the same resolve(), make ExportItems fail closed when CallerFrom returns !ok, and delete the x-catalog-tenant fallback.

triage.reason: Not hygiene: the component's only authentication control simply does not cover this RPC class.
One gRPC call reproduces it.
Production service registered at main.go:64 via RegisterCatalogServer.
The unary interceptor is a genuine mitigation and is credited; it simply does not apply to streams.
Re-read: main.go:52 is the sole interceptor registration, server.go:204 discards the ok, server.go:210 is the metadata fallback, catalog.proto:81 declares the stream.
Ingress: the x-catalog-tenant gRPC metadata read at server.go:210 and the ExportRequest fields at server.go:216, both entirely client-supplied.

scope.established_by: grpc.NewServer is configured with a unary interceptor only, and ExportItems is the one streaming method in the service.
scope.narrowed_by: Server TLS is required (main.go:40-46), so the caller must complete a TLS handshake; that is not authentication of the caller.

searched.for: any grpc.StreamInterceptor, grpc.ChainStreamInterceptor or ServerStream wrapper
searched.found: no matches at all - the grep output was empty

searched.for: whether other handlers treat the CallerFrom ok value differently
searched.found: the unary handlers check it and return Unauthenticated; ExportItems is the only one that discards it with _

searched.for: a health-check style allowlist that might explain a deliberate exemption
searched.found: only /grpc.health.v1.Health/Check is exempted (interceptor.go:81), and no health service is registered

findings.title: SQL injection in store.ExportQuery: the export filter and order_by are concatenated into WHERE and ORDER BY
findings.evidence: ExportQuery builds the statement with fmt.Sprintf, interpolating the tenant into a quoted literal and the caller's filter and order strings into the predicate and sort position: `WHERE tenant_id = '%s' AND (%s)` / `ORDER BY %s` (search.go:110-115). The values come straight off the wire -- `store.ExportQuery(tenantID, req.GetFilter(), req.GetOrderBy())` (server.go:216) -- and the result is handed to the pool as a bare string (postgres.go:226). The file's own allowlist parsers, ParseFilter and ParseOrderBy, are called only from Search (server.go:180 and :184) and never on this path.
findings.impact: Arbitrary SQL as the application's database role, reachable with no credentials at all through the unauthenticated ExportItems stream: full cross-tenant read of every table the role can see, and whatever write or function-execution the role permits.
findings.recommendation: Run the export filter through ParseFilter and the sort through ParseOrderBy exactly as Search does, and bind the tenant as a parameter instead of interpolating it into a quoted literal.

triage.reason: The opposite of pedantic linting: the safe parameterised style is used elsewhere in the same package and abandoned here.
A single ExportItems call with a crafted filter reproduces it deterministically.
No mitigation is being stretched -- ParseFilter/ParseOrderBy exist but are not on this path, which I verified by checking their call sites.
Direct injection path in the function's own logic.
Re-read: search.go:111 is the WHERE line, :112 the ORDER BY line, server.go:216 the call, postgres.go:226 the Query.
Ingress: ExportRequest.filter and .order_by read at server.go:216, unauthenticated per the ExportItems finding.

scope.established_by: ExportQuery returns a formatted string rather than a statement plus arguments, and its one caller passes request fields into it unfiltered.
scope.narrowed_by: Only the export path is affected; Search's own SQL clamps LIMIT/OFFSET to integers and takes ORDER BY from the sortableColumns allowlist.

searched.for: call sites of ParseFilter and ParseOrderBy
searched.found: both are called only from Search (server.go:180, :184); neither appears on the export path

searched.for: whether StreamQuery re-parses or parameterises the statement it is given
searched.found: nothing - it passes the string to p.pool.Query directly at line 226

searched.for: whether the rest of the store uses parameters, to rule out a repo-wide style
searched.found: it does - e.g. the tenant-scoped SELECT at postgres.go:90 and the DELETE at :184 both use $1/$2 placeholders

findings.title: The x-catalog-role request header overrides the role stored on the session
findings.class: privilege escalation via trusted client header (CWE-807)
findings.evidence: resolve() builds the Caller from the looked-up session and then unconditionally replaces the role with a request header if one is present: `if role := metadataValue(ctx, "x-catalog-role"); role != "" { caller.Role = role }` (interceptor.go:67-69). RequireRole compares against exactly that field (interceptor.go:96-99), and admin-only handlers call it (e.g. server.go:153). On the HTTP side the gateway forwards every header matching the `x-catalog-` prefix (http.go:23) and its strippedHeaders map removes only x-catalog-tenant and x-catalog-subject (http.go:27-30) -- x-catalog-role is not stripped.
findings.impact: Any caller holding a valid session, however low-privileged, adds `X-Catalog-Role: admin` and passes every role check in the service. Tenant scoping still comes from the session, so the escalation is within the caller's own tenant -- which is why this is high rather than the top of the scale.
findings.recommendation: Delete the override, or accept it only as a narrowing of roles the session already carries, and add x-catalog-role to the gateway's strippedHeaders.

triage.reason: The override is performed by the interceptor itself, immediately after the authoritative lookup.
One request with an extra header reproduces it.
The gateway's header-stripping mitigation is real and credited -- it just omits this header, which I confirmed by reading the map.
Re-read: interceptor.go:67-68 are the override, http.go:23 the forward prefixes, http.go:27-30 the stripped map with two entries.

findings.title: Plugin refresh downloads and writes the bundle with no checksum check, unlike first install
findings.class: download of code without integrity check (CWE-494)
findings.evidence: installPlugin verifies the bundle against the sha256 recorded in the signed feed before writing it -- `if (sha256(bundle) !== entry.sha256) { throw ... }` (updater.js:48-50). refreshPlugin performs the same download and write for an already-installed plugin with nothing in between: it fetches `entry.updateUrl || entry.url` (updater.js:69), reads the body (:70) and writes it to disk (:74). There is no scheme constraint on updateUrl and no host allowlist. The comment rationalises the omission -- 'The feed entry was checked when the plugin was first added, so this only has to move bytes' -- but the earlier check covered the feed document, not these bytes. Both integrity primitives the component defines are involved: verifyManifest is called only by fetchFeed (updater.js:19) and sha256 only by installPlugin (updater.js:48).
findings.impact: Whoever controls the updateUrl origin -- a hijacked CDN, a stale DNS record, or a plain http:// URL in an otherwise signed feed -- ships arbitrary bytes into the application's plugin directory under a predictable filename, defeating the supply-chain control this module exists to enforce. Reachable from the shipped UI: the renderer's Update button calls plugins.refresh (renderer/app.js:89).
findings.recommendation: Apply the same sha256 comparison in refreshPlugin, re-fetch the signed feed rather than trusting feedCache, and require updateUrl to be https on the plugin host.

Not defense-in-depth: integrity verification is this module's stated purpose.

The feed signature is a working mitigation and is credited; the finding is the bundle bytes it does not cover.
